analysis.one_liner: Requires upfront all-in pricing and bans hidden fees on tickets, lodging, phone, internet, and flights.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced December 4, 2025, was read twice and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it sits with no hearing or vote; it has two Democratic sponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill targets 'junk fees' — mandatory charges that show up after you see an advertised price, like resort fees, ticket service fees, and phone or internet surcharges. It would require companies to show the full price up front, keep advertised prices from changing at checkout, ban excessive or deceptive fees, and disclose how many tickets are held back from public sale. It covers short-term lodging and hotels, ticket sellers, phone, cable, and broadband providers, and adds reporting rules for airline fees like checked bags and seat selection. The FTC, FCC, and Department of Transportation would enforce it, and state attorneys general could sue too.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who books a hotel or short-term rental, buys an event ticket, subscribes to cable, internet, or phone service, or flies. They would see the true total price before buying, get prorated credits when ending a service early, receive full refunds including fees when a ticket is refunded, and learn upfront that a 'speculative' ticket seller does not actually hold the ticket. People whose introductory cable or internet prices expire would get advance notice of the higher rate.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers booking lodging, tickets, phone, internet, flights

how_it_helps.text: Covered businesses must display the total price, including all mandatory fees and government charges, in every ad and at the first price shown, and the price cannot rise between advertisement and checkout [S2].
Businesses may not impose or advertise mandatory fees that are excessive or deceptive, such as fees misrepresented as optional ones you must opt out of [S2].

Ticket sellers must disclose the total number of tickets available for an event at least 72 hours before the first public sale or presale, and refund the full ticket cost including fees; sellers who do not hold the ticket must say so and refund in full if they cannot deliver [S2].

Phone, cable, broadband, and bundled-service providers must show one clear aggregate price on bills and ads, disclose when a promotional price ends and what the post-promotion rate will be, and may not charge early termination fees or bill for unused days after cancellation [S2].

Airlines must report quarterly to the Department of Transportation the revenue they collect from ancillary fees such as checked bags, reservation changes, and seat selection, with the totals published on DOT's website [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Hotels and short-term lodging platforms, ticket sellers, telecom and cable companies, and airlines, which would have to restructure pricing, ads, and billing, and would lose revenue from fees that are currently easy to bury. Fees that regulators find excessive or deceptive could be disallowed entirely, shrinking revenue that companies now book as high-margin add-ons.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hotels, ticket sellers, telecoms, and airlines

drawbacks.text: The 'excessive fee' standard is open-ended: the FTC and courts would judge whether a fee is 'reasonable and proportional to the cost of the good or service', which gives regulators discretion and creates uncertainty for businesses about which fees survive [S2].

Compliance costs fall on all covered companies, including small hotels and independent short-term rental hosts who would need to reprogram listings and ads, and some of that cost could be passed on in base prices [S2].

All-in pricing does not lower prices by itself; a resort fee that becomes part of the visible total is still money you pay, and the bill mainly fixes disclosure rather than banning fees outright [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real, everyday cost: mandatory fees that make advertised prices misleading. Its core benefit is honest pricing, not lower prices, and its 'excessive fee' standard is broad enough that its practical reach would depend on how the FTC writes rules. The main costs are compliance and possible price re-shuffling by the affected industries. On balance the disclosure and refund protections would be worth more to ordinary households than the compliance costs are to the companies, but the open-ended regulatory discretion is a genuine trade-off.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote; the Congress is still in session, so it could still move, but so far nothing has happened.

narrative.text: Senator Blumenthal, joined by Senator Gallego, introduced the Junk Fee Prevention Act on December 4, 2025 [S1][S2].
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S4].
As of the record provided, the committee has taken no further action and no vote has occurred [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no outcome has changed anyone's position: consumers continue paying hidden fees, and the covered industries continue charging them. The bill's fate rests with the Senate Commerce Committee, which has not acted.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Junk Fee Prevention Act on December 4, 2025

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democrats have sponsored the bill so far and no Republicans have signed on; no opposition has been recorded because no hearing or vote has occurred.

industries.industry: Short-term lodging and online booking platforms
industries.note: Hotels, vacation rentals, and booking platforms would have to show the all-in price — including fees like resort or cleaning charges — in every ad and could no longer raise the price at checkout or charge fees found deceptive. Their business model currently relies on low advertised base rates that grow with fees added later.

Ticketing services would have to disclose the total tickets available 72 hours before any sale or presale, refund full cost including fees, and flag speculative listings where they do not hold the ticket. This reduces the fees and tactics that make advertised ticket prices climb at checkout.

Providers would have to show one clear aggregate price on bills and ads, disclose when introductory rates end and what the new rate will be, drop early termination fees, and prorate final bills. Fees like equipment surcharges that pad bills would have to be folded into a visible price.

Airlines would not face new fee bans or disclosure requirements at the point of sale, only quarterly reporting of ancillary fee revenue — bags, changes, seat selection — published by the Department of Transportation. The main cost is reporting and recordkeeping; the transparency could pressure them politically but does not change what passengers pay.

industries.industry: Debt-adjacent fee enforcement (FTC, FCC, state enforcers)
industries.note: The bill gives the FTC and FCC new enforcement authority over mandatory and deceptive fees and lets state attorneys general sue on behalf of residents for damages and restitution, expanding the toolkit of consumer-protection enforcers.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Senate Commerce Committee with a single Democratic cosponsor and no committee action so far. Most private members' bills never get a hearing, and with no Republican support in a chamber where Republicans hold 55 seats, it is unlikely to advance unless leadership schedules it or the issue gains broader cosponsorship; the most likely path is that it waits in committee through the session.
